lesson.title: Learning Without Getting Burned: Bandura's Case for Watching
lesson.summary: Albert Bandura argued that people learn a great deal simply by observing others, without needing to personally experience reinforcement or punishment for every behavior.
lesson.body:
Classical conditioning explains learning through association between stimuli, and operant conditioning explains learning through the direct consequences of one's own behavior. Both are powerful, well-supported accounts, but both share an assumption: that the learner has to personally experience the pairing of stimuli, or personally experience the reinforcement or punishment, for learning to happen. Albert Bandura thought this left out an enormous amount of how people actually learn.

Social learning theory proposes that people can learn new behaviors, attitudes, and even emotional reactions simply by watching other people, called models, without ever performing the behavior themselves or receiving any reinforcement directly. A child doesn't need to touch a hot stove to learn it's dangerous; watching a sibling get burned, or even hearing about it, can be enough.

The key mechanism Bandura emphasized is vicarious reinforcement and vicarious punishment: watching a model receive a reward or a punishment for a behavior changes the observer's own likelihood of performing that behavior later, even though the observer experienced no consequence personally. If you watch a coworker get praised for speaking up in a meeting, you become more likely to speak up yourself; if you watch them get shut down for it, you become less likely.

One of Bandura's most important theoretical moves was separating learning from performance. He argued that observation can produce learning that sits latent, unused, until there is some reason, some motivation, to actually perform it. This distinction matters because it means you can't always tell what someone has learned just by watching what they currently do. Social learning theory doesn't throw out reinforcement and punishment; it keeps them as central forces, but it expands who has to experience them directly, and it opens the door to studying the cognitive steps in between watching and doing, which is exactly what observational learning describes next.
